implementation_notes: rspec-mocks creates the double for you with double('clock') or, better, a verifying double against the real class (instance_double('Clock')) that refuses stubs for methods and arguments the class does not define; the test then configures answers with allow(clock).to receive(:now).and_return(epoch), where and_return(a, b) supplies consecutive values and and_raise configures a failure, and expect(x).to receive(:y).with(z) is the same mechanism used as an assertion. That is the framework's configuration interface; because Ruby objects are open, a partial double on a real object (allow(real).to receive(...)) is the same call.
code_sketch:
clock = instance_double('Clock')
allow(clock).to receive(:now).and_return(epoch, epoch + 31 * 60)

session = Session.new(clock, 30 * 60)
expect(session).to be_expired
expect(clock).to have_received(:now).twice
pitfalls: Per-example lifetime: rspec-mocks removes stubs after each example, so a double stored in a before(:suite)/class-level place cannot be configured that way - keep it per example or build it explicitly.
Stubbing every collaborator methods with a plain double() instead of instance_double() skips verification, so a renamed method keeps the test green.
allow_any_instance_of / any_instance stubs are global mutations that hide injection problems and leak into other examples.

variants.name: Hand-written collaborator class configured with attributes
variants.idiom_name: reusable test collaborator class with attribute-configured answers
variants.implementation_notes: A small class (or a Struct built with Struct.new) implements the collaborator's messages and reads its answers from attributes the test sets, so the double is a normal Ruby object that works the same under Minitest or Test::Unit and needs no framework loaded; because Ruby dispatches on message names only, no interface has to be declared. Prefer it when the role is small, when the double must outlive one example, or when it should also record what it received; keep rspec-mocks for verifying doubles and argument expectations.
variants.code_sketch:
class ConfigurableClock
  attr_accessor :instant, :fail

  def now
    raise Timeout::Error, 'clock unavailable' if fail

    instant
  end
end

clock = ConfigurableClock.new.tap { |c| c.instant = epoch }
pitfalls: Ruby never checks that the double answers the messages the SUT sends, so a missing method fails as a NoMethodError rather than a clear configuration error.
attr_accessor exposes the configuration interface publicly, so production code can configure the double if the object is accidentally wired outside tests.
Sharing one double instance across examples leaks configured answers and recorded calls; build it in a per-example setup block.
